questions.stem: Which of the following best defines labour productivity?
options: Output per employee over a period of time
The percentage of employees who leave each year
The percentage of working days lost to absence
The average wage paid per employee
questions.why: Labour productivity = total output divided by the number of employees.
whyNot: That is labour turnover.
That is absenteeism.
That is average pay, which is a cost measure rather than a productivity measure.

questions.stem: A business employs an average of 50 staff and produces 30,000 units. What is labour productivity?
options: 600 units per employee
0.0017 units
50 units
whyNot: That multiplies the two figures instead of dividing.
That divides employees by output, which is the wrong way round.
That is simply the number of employees.

questions.stem: A business employs an average of 80 staff and 18 left during the year. What is labour turnover?
whyNot: That is the number of leavers, not a percentage of the workforce.
That divides 80 by 18, which is the wrong way round.
That is labour retention, the complement of turnover.

questions.stem: 62 out of an average of 80 employees were employed for the whole year. What is labour retention?
questions.why: (62 / 80) x 100 = 77.5%. Notice it and turnover of 22.5% total 100%, which is a useful arithmetic check.
whyNot: That is labour turnover, the complement of retention.
That is the number of staff retained, not a percentage of the workforce.
That divides 80 by 62, which is the wrong way round.

questions.stem: 80 staff could work 250 days each and 640 staff days were lost to absence. What is the absenteeism rate?
questions.why: Total possible = 80 x 250 = 20,000 staff days. (640 / 20,000) x 100 = 3.2%.
whyNot: That divides 640 by 80, forgetting to multiply by the working days.
That misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.
That uses an incorrect denominator.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct denominator for the absenteeism calculation?
options: Number of employees multiplied by working days in the period
Number of employees only
Number of working days only
Number of employees who were absent at least once
questions.why: The denominator is total staff days possible, which requires both the headcount and the number of working days.
whyNot: Using headcount alone ignores how many days each could have worked.
Using days alone ignores how many people could have worked them.
That would exclude staff who were never absent, distorting the rate.

questions.stem: Replacing one employee costs $2,000 and 18 staff left this year. What is the annual cost of turnover?
questions.why: 18 x $2,000 = $36,000. Costing the turnover is what turns the calculation into analysis.
whyNot: That is the cost of replacing just one employee.
That divides the replacement cost by the number of leavers.
That is the saving from a reduction in turnover, not the current total cost.

questions.stem: Turnover falls from 22.5% to 12% in a business averaging 80 staff, with replacement costing $2,000. Roughly how much is saved each year?
options: About $16,000
About $36,000
About $2,000
questions.why: 22.5% of 80 is 18 leavers and 12% of 80 is about 10, so around 8 fewer leavers at $2,000 each saves roughly $16,000.
whyNot: That is the cost of turnover at the original rate, not the saving.
That is the cost of one replacement.
That overstates the saving by a factor of ten.

questions.stem: Why is zero labour turnover not an ideal target?
options: No new ideas or fresh skills enter, and there is no way to move on poor performers
It would breach employment law in most countries
It always means the business is paying too little
It makes absenteeism impossible to measure
questions.why: The optimum level of turnover is low rather than nil, which is a useful evaluative point.
whyNot: There is no legal requirement for staff to leave.
Zero turnover more often suggests generous conditions than low pay.
Absenteeism is measured independently of turnover.

questions.stem: Which of the following makes comparing turnover figures across industries unreliable?
options: Normal rates differ greatly, so hospitality and retail figures would alarm a manufacturer
Turnover cannot be calculated in service industries
The formula changes from one industry to another
Turnover is only published by listed companies
questions.why: Judge the figure against the industry norm, not against zero.
whyNot: It can be calculated wherever there are employees.
The formula is the same; the norms differ.
Any business can calculate it from its own records.

questions.stem: In Herzberg's terms, why may a pay rise fail to solve high turnover caused by boring work?
options: Pay is a hygiene factor, so it removes dissatisfaction rather than creating motivation
Pay is a motivator, so it fully addresses the cause
Pay has no effect on employee behaviour at all
Boring work is a hygiene factor that only pay can address
questions.why: If the problem is the nature of the work and the absence of responsibility, a pay rise buys a short reprieve without fixing the cause.
whyNot: Herzberg classified pay as a hygiene factor, not a motivator.
Pay clearly affects behaviour; the question is which type of factor it addresses.
The nature of the work relates to motivators such as responsibility and achievement.

questions.stem: Which strategy for improving human resource performance delivers Herzberg's motivators most directly?
options: Empowerment, because it gives employees responsibility for their own work
A pay rise, because money is what employees care about most
Tighter supervision, because it raises standards
Reducing holiday entitlement to increase working days
questions.why: Empowerment delivers responsibility, which Herzberg identified as a genuine motivator, though it needs training and clear boundaries.
whyNot: Pay is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's model.
Closer supervision reduces autonomy and is likely to demotivate.
Cutting entitlements worsens hygiene factors and would raise dissatisfaction.

questions.stem: A business reports turnover of 22.5% overall, made up of 5% among managers and 60% among frontline staff. What is the lesson?
options: Averages hide the distribution, and the two groups represent completely different problems
The overall figure is the only one that matters
The manager figure must have been calculated incorrectly
High frontline turnover is unavoidable and needs no action
questions.why: An average conceals where the problem actually lies, so the remedy has to be aimed at the group with the problem.
whyNot: Acting on the average would spread effort across a group that has no problem.
There is no reason to doubt the calculation; genuine differences between groups are normal.
It may be high by sector standards and still be worth reducing once costed.

questions.stem: Why is employee share ownership only weakly linked to daily behaviour?
options: An individual employee's effort barely moves the share price
Employees are not allowed to own shares in their employer
Share ownership reduces pay
Shares cannot be sold by employees
questions.why: It aligns interests over the long term, but the connection between one person's work today and the share price is too thin to change behaviour much.
whyNot: Employee share schemes are common and lawful.
Share ownership is usually additional to pay rather than a replacement for it.
Schemes normally allow shares to be sold after a holding period.

questions.stem: Why is consulting employees and then ignoring their answer worse than not consulting?
options: It destroys trust, which makes future consultation and change harder
It costs more than genuine consultation
It is illegal in most countries
It increases labour productivity in the short run
questions.why: Consultation only works where it is genuine, because staff judge it by whether their views changed anything.
whyNot: The cost of the consultation is the same; the damage is to trust.
Consultation requirements vary, but ignoring views is not generally unlawful.
It is likely to reduce morale and productivity, not raise it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest limitation of the four human resource measures?
options: They show a symptom, not a cause, so exit interviews and surveys are still needed
They cannot be calculated from company records
They are only relevant to businesses with over 500 employees
They always contradict each other
questions.why: A turnover figure tells you there is a problem, not what it is, and diagnosing before prescribing is what earns the higher marks.
whyNot: They are calculated directly from internal records.
They apply to businesses of any size.
They usually reinforce each other, for example high turnover reducing productivity.
